blocks.prompt: The Drum That Learned to Talk
blocks.text: A drum has three parts. The head is the tight skin on top. The shell is the round body under it. The rim is the ring that holds the head down. When you hit the head, it bends down and springs back up, over and over, very fast. That fast moving is called vibration. The vibration pushes the air. The push travels through the air to your ear, and you hear a boom. You can change the sound. Pull the head tighter and the note goes up. Let it go loose and the note goes down. Big drums make deep, low booms. Little drums make quick, high taps.

blocks.prompt: Nobody Invented the Drum
blocks.text: Nobody invented the drum. People all over the world made one, and most of those people never met each other. Long before anyone built a piano or a guitar, someone stretched an animal skin over a hollow log and hit it. Archaeologists have dug up clay drums in China that are thousands of years old. Here is why a drum works. The skin on top is called the head, and it is pulled tight across the shell. When you strike it, the head bends down and springs back, again and again, hundreds of times every second. That fast back and forth motion is called vibration. The vibrating head shoves the air right next to it. That shove travels outward like a ripple crossing a pond, and it does not stop until it reaches your eardrum, which is a tiny stretched skin of your own. Your eardrum starts vibrating too. Your brain calls that sound. So the drum is doing to the air exactly what the air then does to you. Tighten the head and it springs back faster, so the note climbs higher. Loosen it and the note falls.

blocks.prompt: The Drum You Can Hold a Conversation With
blocks.text: Most drums have one voice. Hit them harder and you get a louder version of the same thud. The talking drum of West Africa is built to do something else. It can slide its voice up and down the way a person's voice does, and a skilled player can use it to send a real message. The drum is shaped like an hourglass, wide at both ends and pinched in the middle, with a drumhead stretched over each end. Leather cords run the whole length of the body, lacing the two heads together. The player tucks the drum under one arm and squeezes. Squeezing pulls the cords. The cords pull the heads tighter. A tighter head springs back faster, and a faster spring means a higher note. Relax the arm and the pitch slides back down. One drum, a whole range of notes, controlled by a hug. That design matters because of the languages spoken nearby. Yoruba is a tone language, which means the pitch of your voice is part of the word itself. Say the same syllable high, then say it low, and you have said two different things. A drummer who can copy those rising and falling pitches can copy the shape of a spoken sentence. A listener who knows both the language and the drum hears words inside the rhythm. Before telephones existed, that was a communication network. A message could cross open country faster than any runner, hopping from village to village, played instead of spoken.

blocks.prompt: The Instrument They Built Out of Garbage
blocks.text: Almost every instrument in an orchestra is old. The violin settled into its modern shape in the 1500s. Flutes are older than writing. Genuinely new instruments almost never appear. Then, on one small island in the Caribbean, people built one out of things other people had thrown away. The story starts with a ban. Carnival in Trinidad ran on drums, and in the 1880s the colonial government outlawed skin drums, nervous about what large crowds of drummers might do. Players adapted. They cut bamboo into lengths of different sizes and pounded them on the ground, tuned by length, and called it tamboo bamboo. In the 1930s the authorities banned that too. So musicians went looking for anything that would ring. Biscuit tins. Paint cans. Trash can lids. Brake drums off old cars. Anyone who could strike something metallic and hold a rhythm was welcome. Somewhere in that scramble, players noticed something that changed everything: when you dent a sheet of metal, the dented patch rings at its own pitch, separate from the metal around it. Different dents, different notes. One piece of steel could hold an entire tune. After the Second World War, steel barrels were easy to find on the island, left behind by the oil industry and by wartime bases. They turned out to be ideal. A builder cuts the barrel down, hammers the flat top into a shallow bowl, then patiently pounds grooved sections into that bowl, each one shaped, sized, and tuned to sound one note. Strike a section and only that section sings. Ellie Mannette, a young tuner in Port of Spain, worked out much of the method and is widely credited with sinking the playing face into a concave dish, which gave the instrument its range and its sweetness. The result is the steelpan, and it is why people say the steelpan is the only acoustic instrument invented in the twentieth century. No company designed it. No laboratory funded it. It was hammered out by teenagers who had been told, twice, that they were not allowed to play. Trinidad and Tobago later named it the national instrument. Steel bands now perform on every continent. And under all of it sits the same physics as the first skin stretched over a hollow log. Hit the thing. Make it vibrate. Push the air.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A string's overtones are whole number multiples
A drumhead's are not: about 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65
Nodes are the still patches where the skin barely moves
Timpani are tuned by a pedal that changes head tension
Players strike about a quarter in from the rim

blocks.prompt: Why a Drum Has No Note, and How the Timpani Cheats
blocks.text: Pluck a guitar string and you hear a note you could sing back. Hit a drum and you hear a thump. Both are objects vibrating, both shove air, both make sound. So why does one carry a pitch and the other does not? The answer is arithmetic, and it explains why the drum spent most of its history as an instrument of rhythm rather than melody. Start with the string. A string is essentially one dimensional. When it vibrates, it does not simply swing as one long arc. It also divides itself in half and vibrates as two arcs, and into thirds, and quarters, and onward. Each pattern is called a mode, and each mode has its own frequency. The elegant part is the math. The half pattern rings at exactly twice the frequency of the whole, the thirds at exactly three times, the quarters at four times. Every mode is a whole number multiple of the lowest one. Your ear takes that tidy stack and fuses it into one definite pitch. Musicians call the stack the harmonic series, and it is the reason strings and pipes can play tunes at all. Now stretch a skin across a hoop. A drumhead is two dimensional, and its modes are far stranger. Instead of neat halves and thirds, the surface can vibrate in rings, in wedges, and in combinations of the two, with still patches called nodes where the skin barely moves. Sprinkle sand on a drumhead and feed it a pure tone and the grains will crawl away from the moving regions and pile along those nodes, drawing the pattern for you to look at. The trouble is the frequencies. A drumhead's modes do not arrive in whole number multiples. On an ideal circular membrane the second mode rings at about 1.59 times the first, the next at about 2.14, then 2.30, then 2.65. Those numbers are not close to 2, 3, and 4, and they are not close to anything else tidy either. Your ear receives a crowd of unrelated frequencies and refuses to fuse them. It reports a thud, a boom, a crash. Not a mistake. Just pitchless. Which raises an obvious question. How does a timpani play in tune? An orchestra tunes its timpani to real notes, and composers write real melodies for them. The kettle is the trick, along with where the player strikes. A timpani head is not free. It sits over a sealed bowl of air, and that trapped air loads the skin, dragging certain modes down in frequency. The air outside the head does the same. Meanwhile the player strikes not in the center but roughly a quarter of the way in from the rim, a spot that barely feeds the useless lowest mode while pouring energy into the modes above it. Between the air loading and the striking point, those upper modes land near ratios of 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3. Double them and you get 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. That is a harmonic series with its bottom note missing, and the ear, which has spent a lifetime completing such patterns, supplies the missing fundamental and hears a pitch that is not physically there. So a timpani is a drum that has been argued into behaving like a string. The bowl, the striking spot, the tension, the exact thickness of the head: all of it exists to bully an unruly two dimensional surface into the arithmetic of a one dimensional one. It is one of the few places in music where you can watch people fight physics and win on points. Every other drum on Earth simply shrugs and thumps. And we built most of the world's music on top of the thumping anyway.
